questions_and_answers.question_text: How do you say in Chinese that something is a certain color?
Which negative may be used with adjectival verbs, and why?
What kind of le is used in a sentence whose verb is adjectival?
What is the literal meaning of nánkàn?
Which verb means "to be old in years," as opposed to jiù?
Write the Chinese for "This vase is blue."
What happens to the meaning of an adjectival verb when it becomes a process verb?

answers.answer_text: The verb meaning is often changed — as in Wǒde yǔsǎn jiù le, "My umbrella has become old."

questions_and_answers.question_text: What is jiù NOT used to mean?
What is ǎi NOT used to mean?

answers.answer_text: "Short in length" — the verb duǎn is used for that.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "The sky has darkened."

articles.text:
Notes on Additional Required Vocabulary

10. bái        to be white
11. hēi        to be black
12. huáng      to be yellow, to be brown
13. lǜ         to be green
14. jiù        to be old, to be used, to be worn
15. xīn        to be new
16. gāo        to be tall
17. ǎi         to be short (of stature)
18. gāoxìng    to be happy
19. nánkàn     to be ugly
20. yìbǎ yǔsǎn one umbrella
21. kàn        to read, to look at, to visit

Colors: Adjectival verbs of color behave somewhat differently than other adjectival verbs, such as guì and dà. To say in Chinese that something is a certain color, such as blue, you say that it is "a blue one."

Zhèige huāpíng shi lánde.        This vase is blue.
Nèiběn shū shi hēide.            That book is black.

Adjectival verbs: As you learned in BIO, adjectival verbs are state verbs and as such can be made negative only with bù. If the marker le is used in a sentence whose verb is adjectival, the marker is new-situation le.

Zuótian wǒ kànle hěn duō         Yesterday I saw a lot of vases.
huāpíng. Dōu bú guì.             None of them were expensive.
Nǐde háizi hěn gāo le!           Your son is tall now!

Like many other state verbs, adjectival verbs may become process verbs. When this happens, the verb meaning is often changed.

Wǒde yǔsǎn jiù le.               My umbrella has become old.
Tiān hēi le.                     The sky has become black (has darkened).

Jiù is the verb "to be old," "to be used," "to be worn," as opposed to xīn, "to be new." Jiù is not used to mean old in years, or aged. (The verb lǎo means "to be old in years." Niánqīng means "to be young.")

Ǎi is the verb "to be short (in stature)," as opposed to gāo, "to be tall." Ǎi is not used to mean "short in length." (The verb duǎn means "to be short in length." Cháng means "to be long.")

Nánkàn, "to be ugly," literally, "to be hard to look at": This is a very blunt way to describe unattractiveness.
